Article Title: 'No, I won't let our baby be thrown into river': Sonia recalls loss of first child before Rahul
Article Text:
Before Rahul, Sonia and Rajiv lost first child; memoir reveals details (Picture from X)

NEW DELHI: In September 1968, the Gandhi household was filled with joy when Sonia Gandhi announced her pregnancy. Even the usually stern Indira Gandhi broke into a rare display of affection, embracing her daughter-in-law Sonia Gandhi and exclaiming, “One big baby having another baby!”But the happiness was short-lived.Sonia gave birth to a premature baby boy on January 18, 1969, two months before her due date. Initially overjoyed, the family was soon devastated by the newborn’s death.In her newly released memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia recounts the deeply personal tragedy for the first time. She writes that the baby was buried by her husband Rajiv Gandhi and brother-in-law Sanjay Gandhi at Feroze Gandhi’s farmhouse in Mehrauli.“I heard the baby's first cry as he was placed in the incubator. Later Rajiv took me to see him, a tiny, perfectly formed boy, with thick, black hair and long, slim fingers. We gazed at him together, Rajiv's arm around my shoulder. We fell in love with him immediately,” she writes.Doctors had warned Rajiv that the baby’s chances of survival were uncertain. At 6:30 am, he was informed that the newborn had died.“With Amie Aunty beside him, he broke it gently to me when at 6:30 in the morning the end came.‘No it was not possible! Why, why,’ I kept asking. Both of us were shocked and heartbroken, we held each other tight. I cried my heart out, and Rajiv, in spite of his ‘stiff upper lip’ upbringing, also wept copiously,” she recalls.Indira, who was away on a tour, cut short her visit and rushed to the hospital.“She embraced us, her eyes red and swollen, and sat with us for a long time. She wanted to remain with us, she said, but had to complete her tour engagement. She left early the next morning, full of sorrow: She, too, had so looked forward to the happy event.”The family then faced the difficult question of the newborn’s last rites. Sonia writes that, according to Hindu tradition, a newborn could not be cremated and was traditionally released into a river.However, the thought brought back a disturbing memory of seeing a swollen male body trapped near the Okhla barrage, with scavenging dogs trying to pull it out.“‘No,’ I whispered. ‘No matter what, I'm not going to allow our baby to be thrown into the river.’...’No, I couldn't do that to my baby, no matter how sacred the river was,’ I said, breaking into sobs. How could I consent to do something that seemed to me so alien and heartless to my tiny child, already deprived of his chance to live?”The family eventually decided to bury the child at Feroze Gandhi’s farmhouse in Mehrauli.“It was a painful and agonising option, but there was no other way. Rajiv came back to the hospital and told me that he and Sanjay had buried the little one deep under a beautiful pink bougainvillea bush, then in full bloom on the left side along the inner boundary wall," she recounts.“For a long time we'd pause and place a flower over the spot each time we went there. It didn't assuage our pain, but we had to accept the inevitable,” she writes.Sonia also recalls how Indira had closely monitored her pregnancy, advising her on diet, walks and exercise. She writes that she had no major discomfort, apart from missing Italian food and developing a craving for jamun, phalsa and Fanta, sometimes drinking twelve glasses a day.The loss left her depressed and struggling with feelings of inadequacy and guilt. The pain was compounded by a right-wing opposition newspaper publishing an article titled, "Indira Gandhi failed in her attempt to become the grandmother of a bastard child."“The venom of those words scarred my heart. How could people be so cruel? What had I done to deserve such malice? The hurt caused by that spiteful comment added to the heartbreak of my loss and to my feeling of inadequacy,” she writes.In October 1969, Sonia told Rajiv she was pregnant again. “Thrilled but anxious”, she gave birth to their second child, Rahul Gandhi , on June 19, 1970.
Article Summary: Sonia gave birth to a premature baby boy on January 18, 1969, two months before her due date. In her newly released memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia recounts the deeply personal tragedy for the first time. She writes that the baby was buried by her husband Rajiv Gandhi and brother-in-law Sanjay Gandhi.

Article Title: Clinton's 'old habit', 'arrogant' Sarkozy & 'real star' Diana: Sonia's candid accounts of world leaders

Sarkozy's love life and an amused Sonia

NEW DELHI: Former Congress president Sonia Gandhi recalls in her memoir how then-US president Bill Clinton, during his 2000 India visit, would occasionally be seen "surreptitiously sizing up the more striking women" at a reception hosted in his honour. The Monica Lewinsky scandal may have faded from the headlines by then, but, as Sonia writes, "old habits die hard".The anecdote is among several candid recollections of Sonia's interactions with global leaders and prominent personalities, including former French president Nicolas Sarkozy and the late Princess Diana, in her newly released memoir, Belonging: A Journey Of Love.Recalling Clinton's 2000 visit, Sonia writes about meeting the then US president at the Sheraton hotel, where he was staying with his daughter Chelsea and his delegation. She had called on him along with then-foreign minister."Friendly, informal, and exuding confidence, he appeared more keen to give us his own views and predictions about Kashmir- 'a nuclear flashpoint', in his words, 'one of the most dangerous places on earth'--than to pay attention to our point of view," she writes.Sonia also recounts a reception hosted by then-prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee in Clinton's honour, where she noticed the former US president occasionally looking at women in attendance."The Monica Lewinsky scandal had subsided a little by then, but old habits die hard; at the reception held by Prime Minister Vajpayee in his honour, I noticed him every now and then surreptitiously sizing up the more striking women present," she writes.Sonia also shares an interesting account of Nicolas Sarkozy's 2008 visit to India, when the French president travelled without his then partner, Carla Bruni."It was said that he (Sarkozy) had been advised not to bring her (Bruni) because they were unmarried which would have been awkward at official functions," she writes.At a banquet, the wife of then vice-president Mohammad Ansari, seated next to Sarkozy, began asking him about his relationship with Bruni, including whether he planned to marry her and whether a date had been fixed."President Sarkozy seemed unperturbed by the cross-examination, even eager to share details of his love life, answering all her questions while continuously messaging his Carla on his phone," Sonia recalls.The couple made a joint appearance in India on a subsequent visit, attending a private dinner hosted by then prime minister Manmohan Singh and his wife.By then, Sarkozy and Bruni had married. Sonia remembers the French president as being visibly besotted with his wife, who had been a popular singer and songwriter in Europe as well as a top model."All eyes were on her as she glided into the room in an elegant long gown, graceful and slim, demure and blue-eyed," she writes.However, Sonia's impression of the evening was not limited to Bruni's appearance. She also recalls Sarkozy holding forth on India's responsibilities while speaking to Manmohan Singh."He was obviously besotted with his tall and beautiful wife of Italian and French descent, who had been a popular singer and songwriter in Europe, as well as a top model. All eyes were on her as she glided into the room in an elegant long gown, graceful and slim, demure and blue-eyed," she writes."She spoke cordially but infrequently--while her husband held forth, expounding his views to our prime minister on what India should do in what I felt was a rather arrogant manner, unmindful of the fact that he was talking to someone more senior, more experienced and more knowledgeable," she adds.Among the most personal recollections in the memoir are Sonia's encounters with the British royal family, particularly Princess Diana.She writes that members of the British royal family had shared a friendship with the Nehru-Gandhi family over generations, while Rajiv Gandhi had got along well with Prince Charles."The real star of that family had of course been Princess Diana: Tall and slim, with large blue eyes, an enchanting smile, and a magnetic personality. I can never forget how ravishing she was as a bride when Rajiv and I attended their wedding in 1981. But when they came to India in 1992, it was evident that things were not going well in the marriage," Sonia writes.She recalls an informal meeting with the royal couple during their 1992 India visit, on the same day Diana famously posed alone on a bench in front of the Taj Mahal, later popularly known as the 'love bench'."On the very day she famously posed alone on what I call the 'love bench' in front of the Taj Mahal, they had come over for a late tea. Prince Charles was forthcoming and amusing, but she appeared morose, though looking wonderful in a striking red and purple two-piece suit. We chatted about what she had seen and liked on her visit," she writes.Sonia's mother, who was visiting at the time, was keen to meet the princess. Her daughter Priyanka was equally eager to introduce her 'Nonna' (grandmother) to Diana.When Diana wondered why Sonia's mother was so quiet, Priyanka immediately explained that she had been told not to speak because she only knew Italian."Diana burst out laughing and turned immediately to my mother, holding out her hand, "Piacere, comne stai?" ("Pleased to meet you, how are you?"), trying to pronounce the words in the correct Italian accent, though using the informal form of address, but with such warmth and charm that we all melted," Sonia recalls.The meeting ended on another warm note. As the royal couple were leaving, Diana stopped midway, turned around and waved to Sonia's mother."After tea and more chat, we were seeing them off to their car when she stopped halfway, turned back to wave to my mother, and called out, 'Ciao. Nonna!' After I presented the royal couple with my book Rajiv, she wrote to me, telling me how much she had admired my husband," Sonia writes.Sonia also recounts a later meeting with Diana in London, when she was invited for tea with the royal couple. She remembers arriving in a black suit with a white collar and joking, "I am feeling like a crow!"On another occasion, she unexpectedly came across Diana at a hairdresser's. Recognising the princess sitting next to her, Sonia decided to pass her a discreet note."I scribbled a word and passed it on to her, and the next second realised that instead of 'Hi', I had written 'Hye'. How I wished I could have snatched back the note! But it was too late; she had already put it into her handbag," she recalls.The two exchanged a few words in hushed tones, careful not to attract attention. It was the last time Sonia met Diana.Reflecting on the public scrutiny surrounding the late princess, Sonia says Diana faced considerable criticism during her lifetime, with many questioning why she appeared unhappy despite her privileged position."There was a lot of criticism of her at that time: She was spoilt and complaining; she had everything; why was she behaving as if she had been wronged? I must say I felt for her throughout, and still do," Sonia writes.
Article Summary: Sonia Gandhi's memoir, Belonging: A Journey Of Love, is out now. She recalls her interactions with world leaders, including Bill Clinton and Princess Diana. She also recalls Nicolas Sarkozy's 2008 visit to India without his then partner, Carla Bruni.

Article Title: What made Sonia Gandhi turn down PM post after UPA’s 2004 victory? Memoir revisits moment
Article Text:

'Sonia, be true to yourself': What made her change her mind

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Sonia Gandhi has revealed what went through her mind when she decided against becoming prime minister after the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) won the 2004 Lok Sabha elections.In her newly released memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia recalls how she eventually listened to her "inner voice" and decided to turn down the top post, despite initially being expected to lead the government. She also explains why she chose Manmohan Singh to become prime minister, describing him as a leader of "unquestionable" integrity with a deep understanding of governance.The memoi revisits the crucial political decision that shaped the UPA government's first term. Sonia also shares details of the discussions with senior Congress leaders and her final conversation with her son, Rahul Gandhi, before announcing her decision.Also Read| 'I'd quake in my seat': Sonia Gandhi recalls Indira Gandhi's temper, early days as bride in memoir Sharing an excerpt from the memoir in an article published by The Indian Express, Sonia Gandhi recalled the moment she finally resolved not to become prime minister."My mind suddenly cleared itself of the last shreds of doubt. “Sonia, be true to yourself,” I could hear myself say.“You’ve always known it. Just leave it!” From Belonging - on the decision not to become Prime Minister," she wrote in a post on X.In the book, she describes how she woke up a few hours later and went straight to Rahul's room to tell him about her decision."I woke up in a few hours, went straight to my son’s room, and knocked on the door. “I’ve made up my mind. I’m going to stick to my stand,” I told him. He stepped up to me and with his arms around me said, “It’s the right decision.”"The CPP President also recalls returning to the Congress Parliamentary Party meeting after making up her mind."I enter the hall to thunderous applause. The members of Par­liament stand up in their places, thumping their palms on the wooden ledges in front of them. I find my place at the centre of the long table for the leaders of the party and remain standing till someone gestures for them to stop, and we all take our seats," she wrote.Also Read| 'Should've called it Whitewashing, not Belonging': BJP mocks Sonia Gandhi's memoir After deciding against taking the top post, Sonia had to identify someone who could lead the new government. She says several senior Congress leaders were qualified for the position, but Manmohan Singh stood out."There were several senior colleagues, seasoned and qualified for the post, who would have been more than willing to accept it but amongst all of them was one who had long been in my sight as a person above reproach, and possessed a deep and consummate understanding of governance. That was Dr Manmohan Singh, a member of the Congress Working Committee," she writes.Sonia points to Singh's experience as finance minister in the early 1990s, when he introduced economic reforms under the government of then prime minister PV Narasimha Rao.She also believed his appointment would reassure people about the UPA's economic policies, particularly as the alliance was supported by the Communist parties."He was not allied to any camp in the party. Over a period of time, the Congress had been painted as being left of centre, and our government would now be supported by the Communist parties as well. I thought Dr Manmohan Singh would assuage the doubts of many about our ability to manage and continue the policies that had been begun years ago," she says.Sonia also recalls Manmohan Singh's personal journey, from a village in Punjab, now in Pakistan, to the universities of Oxford and Cambridge. She describes him as a hardworking scholar and technocrat who had overcome considerable hardship."Aside from all his accomplishments as a scholar and technocrat, what I knew best about Dr Singh was that he had a kind and compassionate heart, and his integrity unquestionable," she writes.She says she was convinced that the country would be in safe hands under his leadership. After consulting senior colleagues, she proposed his name. They did not oppose the choice.Manmohan Singh was approached privately about taking up the position. Although he initially declined, the CPP President says he was eventually persuaded to accept it.Sonia Gandhi also recounts the events of May 18, 2004, when she went to Rashtrapati Bhawan to stake the UPA's claim to form the government. She was accompanied by Singh.Recalling her arrival, she describes an emotional moment as she walked through the building where she had earlier visited with her mother-in-law, former prime minister Indira Gandhi, and her husband, Rajiv Gandhi."I felt a sudden surge of emotion as our cars pulled up at the entrance. I'd been there many times before with my mother-in-law and with Rajiv, but this time I was walking through the long, dark corridors of Rashtrapati Bhawan for a different purpose," she writes.After the meeting, the two returned to her residence at 10, Janpath. Sonia Gandhi says she did not discuss the prime ministership with Singh, who, like everyone else, assumed she would take the post."We returned from Rashtrapati Bhawan to my home at 10, Janpath. I saw Dr Singh to his car. There had been no discussion about the prime ministership between the two of us on the drive back nor had there been before that. I said nothing to him even now. He had quite naturally assumed, like everyone else, that it would be me," she recalls.Sonia Gandhi has recalled how Pranab Mukherjee hinted at his "long-held desire" to become prime minister during a 2010 conversation, when he suggested that "it was time for a change at the top", according to her newly released memoir.Rejecting criticism that she was a "back seat driver" during the UPA years, Sonia said she respected Manmohan Singh's position as prime minister and believed it was her duty to defer to him, even when they disagreed."Further. I was determined not to be under any circumstance the cause of a misunderstanding that could give our opponents occasion to rejoice and weaken our government," she writes in the book, released on Tuesday.Also Read| ‘Not a political book, but a personal one’: Sonia Gandhi ahead of memoir release Belonging: A Journey of Love traces Sonia Gandhi's life from her childhood in post-war Italy to her marriage to Rajiv Sonia Gandhi and her eventual move to India.Born in Italy, she was 19 and studying in Cambridge, England, when she met Rajiv in 1965. The couple married on February 25, 1968. The memoir recounts her introduction to Indira Gandhi and her efforts to adjust to life in India, including learning Hindi, wearing saris and adapting to Indian food and culture.It also revisits the personal tragedies that shaped her life, including the death of Sanjay Gandhi in a plane crash, Indira Gandhi's assassination in 1984 and Rajiv Gandhi's assassination in 1991.Among the most personal accounts is her recollection of the night Rajiv was assassinated in Sriperumbudur, Tamil Nadu, on May 21, 1991. She recalls how their daughter Priyanka broke the news to her and how she struggled to accept that her husband was dead.The memoir also recounts Rahul's concerns about his father's security. Two months before the assassination, Rahul had warned his mother: "If something isn’t done about Pa’s security, I know I’ll soon have to come back for his funeral."
Article Summary: Congress leader Sonia Gandhi has revealed what went through her mind when she decided against becoming prime minister. In her newly released memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia recalls how she eventually listened to her "inner voice" and decided to turn down the top post. She also explains why she chose Manmohan Singh to become prime minister, describing him as a leader of "unquestionable" integrity.

Article Title: 'Should've called it Whitewashing, not Belonging': BJP mocks Sonia Gandhi's memoir
Article Text:
Sonia detailed her lifestory in the memoir

What Sonia Gandhi's memoir is about

NEW DELHI: The BJP on Tuesday criticised Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi over her memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, with party spokesperson CR Kesavan accusing her of attempting to "whitewash" the "historical wrongs" of the Nehru-Gandhi family and the Congress.In a series of post on X, Kesavan said the book should have been titled 'Whitewashing' instead of 'Belonging', alleging that its purpose was to sugarcoat the historical wrongs committed by the Nehru-Gandhi family and camouflage the Congress party's "cardinal sins".Referring to Sonia Gandhi's account of crying over the demolition of the Babri Masjid, Kesavan questioned whether she had also expressed grief over the 1984 anti-Sikh riots and the killing of thousands of people during the violence. "Did Sonia Gandhi even shed one tear for when the gurdwaras were attacked and innocent people, thousands of innocent people, were violently killed during the 1984 Sikh massacre which happened under the Congress rule," he said.Kesavan also referred to the Batla House encounter, alleging that Sonia Gandhi had wept for the accused, and questioned whether she had expressed similar grief for CRPF personnel killed in the line of duty."Did Sonia Gandhi even shed a single tear for the brave CRPF jawans who were martyred in the line of duty when protecting our nation and people?" he asked.He further questioned whether the memoir would address the 2008 Mumbai terror attacks and the Congress-led UPA government's response to them."Did Sonia Gandhi cry when innocent lives were lost during the horrendous 26/11 terror attacks which happened under the Congress rule? Will Sonia Gandhi's book answer?" Kesavan said, accusing the UPA government of failing to retaliate against the attacks.The BJP spokesperson also criticised Sonia Gandhi's account of the Emergency imposed by then prime minister Indira Gandhi in 1975. He accused her of attempting to justify and normalise the period, during which fundamental rights were suspended and press freedoms curtailed."The way in which Sonia Gandhi has tried to justify and normalise Indira Gandhi imposing the notorious Emergency which murdered our Constitution and suspended fundamental rights is indeed most shocking and appalling," he said.Also read: What made Sonia Gandhi turn down PM post after UPA’s 2004 victory? Memoir revisits moment Kesavan also referred to former external affairs minister K Natwar Singh’s 2014 autobiography, One Life Is Not Enough, questioning Sonia Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra’s visit to his residence ahead of its release. He asked whether her memoir would shed light on the meeting and the events surrounding the formation of the UPA government in May 2004."Will Smt. Sonia Gandhi's memoir also reveal the truth behind her sudden visit to late Shri. K. Natwar Singh’s residence before his book was to be published? Excerpts from Shri. K. Natwar Singh’s 2014 autobiography ‘One Life Is Not Enough’ clearly states how uneasy and uncomfortable the Nehru-Gandhi family was about his account of certain events in May 2004, before the UPA Government was sworn in," Kesavan posted on X.He further questioned why Sonia Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra had met Natwar Singh after eight and a half years and what Sonia Gandhi was apprehensive about him writing on the events leading to the UPA government's formation.Other NDA leaders also took aim at Sonia Gandhi over the memoir. JD(U) MP Sanjay Kumar Jha questioned her account of declining the Prime Minister's post in 2004, claiming that Samajwadi Party leader Mulayam Singh Yadav had refused to support her candidature. “This is a controversial matter as well. While managing numbers, what we know is that Mulayam Singh Yadav had refused to support her. Otherwise, there was a full attempt to become the PM,” Jha said.On her remarks about the Emergency, he said, “She was the PM of the country. Saying that a few people advised her is surprising.”BJP MP Rahul Sinha dismissed the significance of the memoir, saying, “Sonia Gandhi’s writings will not make any difference; nobody is going to read it.” He also criticised her support for Indira Gandhi despite the Emergency and the imprisonment of citizens.Meanwhile, Uttar Pradesh minister Dinesh Pratap Singh claimed that then President APJ Abdul Kalam had refused to swear Sonia Gandhi in as Prime Minister because of her foreign origin. “President Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam refused to swear in Sonia Gandhi due to her foreign origins. Later, this entire incident was portrayed as a resignation,” he said.Titled Belonging: A Journey of Love, the memoir traces Sonia Gandhi's childhood in post-war Italy, her relationship with Rajiv Gandhi while they were at Cambridge, and her life in India. It also recounts the assassinations of Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi.The memoir, which hit bookstores across India on Tuesday, also revisits the crucial political decision that shaped the UPA government's first term. Sonia also shared details of the discussions with senior Congress leaders and her final conversation with her son, Rahul Gandhi, before announcing her decision.In the memoir, Sonia also looks back at her first year as a bride in the Gandhi family, recalling her experiences of living with her mother-in-law, former prime minister Indira Gandhi.She describes Indira Gandhi's occasional outbursts of anger as among the "most alarming" aspects of that period. Recalling one incident, Sonia writes that a staff member who had repeatedly forgotten to remind her mother-in-law about an important appointment was made to stand in a corner of the room, while others hurried past, feeling embarrassed."What I found most alarming was my mother-in-law's occasional explosions of temper. They could freeze the staff into numbness," she wrote. In another instance, Sonia recalled noticing a "kurta-dhoti-clad individual standing immobile in the corner, staring at the wall".She also gave details on why she turned down PM post after UPA victory in 2004.Read more: Sonia recalls Indira's temper, early days as bride in memoir
Article Summary: BJP spokesperson CR Kesavan accuses Sonia Gandhi of attempting to "whitewash" the "historical wrongs" of the Nehru-Gandhi family and the Congress. Kesavan also questioned whether she had expressed grief over the 1984 anti-Sikh riots and the killing of thousands of people during the violence.

What the 2027 contest will turn on

The hills have eyes.And no one needs to remember that more than the parties aiming to win Uttarakhand’s upcoming elections next year.The Pushkar Singh Dhami-led BJP government, has on more than a few occasions proclaimed that they are set to aim for a historic ‘hat-trick’ in the ‘Devbhoomi’. At a recent event in Dehradun, Union home minister Amit Shah set an ambitious target of winning more than 65 of the state's 70 assembly seats. He said the BJP was determined to return to power for a third consecutive term and ensure that the "voice of Uttarakhand" reaches Congress leader Rahul Gandhi.But can the BJP script another first by securing a third consecutive term in a state where governments traditionally changed every five years? Or can the Congress capitalise on anti-incumbency against the Dhami government to wrest back power and add another state to its tally?The BJP enters the election contest on the back of a historic victory in 2022, when it won 47 of Uttarakhand's 70 assembly seats to secure a second consecutive term for the first time since the state's formation in 2000. However, the victory came with some caveats. The party's tally fell sharply from the 57 seats it had won in 2017, while the Congress improved its count from 11 to 19. Although the BJP retained a comfortable majority, both its seat tally and vote share declined. The Congress, meanwhile, made gains but failed to mount a serious challenge to the BJP's hold on power.That gap between retaining power and losing ground is central to the 2027 contest.The BJP aims to defend its record and create history while containing local discontent; the Congress will have to demonstrate that its criticism can translate into organisation, candidates and a coherent alternative.Uttarakhand is also a state where narrow margins have shaped constituency results, making it a state where local politics and national political sentiments both need to be paid heed to.For its first four elections, the state changed hands every time. Congress won 36 seats in 2002, the BJP 35 in 2007, Congress edged ahead 32 to 31 in 2012, and the BJP took 57 in 2017.The year 2022 proved to be historic for BJP as they became the first party to get a consecutive term in the state, even as their vote share slipped from 46.5 to 44.3 per cent while Congress rose from about 33.5 to nearly 38.The BJP enters 2027 legislative assembly elections wanting to retain the ‘Devbhoomi’, consistently highlighting their work within its boundaries and reiterating their claim of making it the cultural capital of the country.The party’s manifesto is sure to highlight: PM Narendra Modi’s national appeal, chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami ’s state-level leadership and the promise that having the same party in power at the Centre and in the state can accelerate development. The BJP is expected to make this double-engine argument a central part of its campaign, pointing to infrastructure projects, road connectivity, pilgrimage tourism and welfare schemes as evidence of what this political alignment can deliver.The party has already signalled that Dhami will remain its face in the 2027 election. National president Nitin Nabin indicated this during his May visit, while also stressing the need for a strategy tailored to Uttarakhand rather than one copied from other states. The leadership arrangement allows the BJP to combine the Prime Minister’s popularity with Dhami’s visibility as the head of the state government. It also gives the party a way to frame the election around continuity, arguing that another term would allow ongoing projects and policies to be carried forward.The party is also working to consolidate its social coalition across the state’s varied electorate. Uttarakhand’s political arithmetic includes upper-caste communities, particularly Brahmins and Rajputs, Scheduled Castes, OBC groups, and communities in the Terai and plains with distinct local and regional interests. The BJP’s challenge is to retain its existing support while expanding its appeal among groups where the Congress and other parties remain competitive. Its outreach to Dalit communities has acquired particular visibility amid the political dispute over the alleged purification ritual at Haldwani’s Ramlila Maidan after Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge’s rally. Both parties have sought to engage Scheduled Caste voters in the aftermath of the controversy.Women and younger voters are also important to the party’s calculations. Reports on the BJP’s preparations suggest that it is considering additional welfare announcements aimed at women, alongside measures to address youth employment and migration. Its outreach has also included ex-servicemen and members of the Sikh community.The BJP’s development narrative is closely linked to its emphasis on religious identity and pilgrimage infrastructure. The Uniform Civil Code, implemented in January 2025, is among the Dhami government’s most prominent policy initiatives. The party has also highlighted the development of religious sites, expansion of tourism infrastructure and preparations for the Haridwar Kumbh.Organisation is set to be another pillar of their strategy, during his September visit to Haldwani, Nabin called on party workers to strengthen the booth-level network and work towards winning every booth. Their emphasis is not simply on mobilising workers closer to polling day, but on maintaining contact with voters, communicating government schemes and identifying constituencies where the party needs to improve its performance.The party is also considering a generational reset in its candidate selection. A TOI report said the BJP is weighing a greater emphasis on younger leaders and women, with performance, voter connect, public acceptance and organisational strength likely to determine ticket allocation. The party has conducted surveys to assess its sitting MLAs, and internal discussions suggest that 20-25% of them could lose their tickets if they receive poor feedback from their constituencies. State BJP president Mahendra Bhatt has maintained that winnability will be the key criterion.The BJP has also sought to make voter-list revision part of its political messaging around identity and demographic change. At a party meeting in Dehradun in June, state president Mahendra Bhatt urged workers to participate actively in the revision of electoral rolls and ensure that those the party described as “infiltrators” and other ineligible persons were removed. “Only the original people of Devbhoomi should decide the government," he said. The remarks reflect how the BJP is linking its appeal around Uttarakhand’s cultural identity with questions of who belongs in the state and who should shape its political future.Taken together, these moves show that the BJP is approaching 2027 with a campaign built around continuity, development, cultural identity and a tighter electoral organisation. But a third term will depend on whether these themes can hold up against the everyday concerns of voters. Questions of jobs, recruitment, migration, land rights and public services are unlikely to disappear simply because the party has sharpened its campaign machinery. For the BJP, the challenge is not only to make history, but to prevent local discontent from becoming a vote against it.The Congress did improve their performance in the 2022 elections but the reality is that they still lost. To make a comeback in the region, Congress will have to not only identify local discontent and areas of vulnerability, but also build a campaign that can carry those issues across the state and maintain coordination among leaders with competing political interests.The party has begun its organisational preparations. On November 2, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi met senior Uttarakhand leaders in New Delhi, including state unit chief Ganesh Godiyal, leader of the opposition Yashpal Arya and senior leaders Pritam Singh and Harak Singh Rawat. Congress general secretary (organisation) K C Venugopal and state in-charge Kumari Selja also attended the meeting, which focused on the party’s strategy for the 2027 assembly elections.The meeting was accompanied by a sharper attack on the BJP government. Kharge accused the state government of failing on law and order, women's safety and accountability, while Venugopal raised allegations of corruption, land grabs, environmental mismanagement and irregularities in recruitment examinations. The party also invoked the Ankita Bhandari case, which is sure to take centre stage in their rejection of the Centre.The murder of 19-year-old Ankita Bhandari in September 2022 remains one of the most politically sensitive issues in Uttarakhand. Bhandari, who worked as a receptionist at the Vanantra resort near Rishikesh, was murdered by resort owner Pulkit Arya and two employees. All three were convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment in May 2025. But the convictions have not brought an end to the family’s campaign for answers about the alleged involvement of an influential person, referred to as a “VIP”, in the circumstances leading to her murder.The controversy has acquired a more direct political dimension because Ankita’s parents have publicly named BJP leader Dushyant Kumar Gautam in their allegations. Gautam, who was appointed governor of Sikkim in October, has denied any involvement and initiated defamation proceedings against those accusing him. The family has demanded that his appointment be put on hold until the investigation into the alleged VIP angle is completed.The family’s protests have also brought the case back into the national political spotlight. On October 14, Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra joined Ankita’s parents at a sit-in near India Gate, where the family was protesting against Gautam’s appointment. Hours later, Delhi Police detained the parents and several Congress leaders; they were released the following morning. On November 4, the parents staged another sit-in near Rajghat and were removed by police.For the Congress, the case has become a prominent part of its challenge to the BJP government on women's safety and accountability. For the ruling party, the continuing protests and the questions raised by Ankita’s family have kept an unresolved controversy in public view, even after the murder trial concluded. As the state approaches another election, the issue is no longer limited to the crime itself; it also concerns the credibility and progress of the investigation into the alleged VIP angle, the family's demand for answers and the government's response to their campaign.The cancellation of the Uttarakhand Subordinate Services Selection Commission’s graduate-level examination in September 2025, after a paper leak was confirmed at an examination centre in Haridwar, renewed questions about the credibility of the recruitment process. More than one lakh candidates had appeared for an examination for 416 posts, and the cancellation triggered protests. The episode also raised questions about the implementation of the state’s 2023 anti-cheating law, which had been introduced after earlier recruitment controversiesPeople leave remote hill villages not only for jobs, but also for better access to education, healthcare, transport and other basic services. The government has cited efforts to encourage reverse migration, but claims of improvement need to be measured against reliable data on village populations, employment and public services. The issue is not simply whether people are returning, but whether they can build sustainable lives in the hills.The 2025 amendment to Uttarakhand’s land laws restricted the purchase of agricultural and horticultural land by people from outside the state in 11 hill districts. While the government has presented this as a measure to protect local interests, campaigners argue that exemptions and the treatment of urban areas leave important gaps.The debate reflects a wider concern over local control of land and resources, and whether the aspirations behind Uttarakhand’s creation in 2000 have been fulfilled. Gairsain, designated as the summer capital, remains central to this discussion, particularly for those who believe development and administration have yet to reach remote hill regions.The Uttarakhand Kranti Dal (UKD), closely associated with the statehood movement, continues to represent some of these concerns. It had four MLAs in the first Assembly in 2002, but its representation declined sharply in subsequent elections. Its decision to field candidates in 2027 signals an attempt to reclaim the debate over regional identity and local rights, though its electoral influence remains limited.Uttarakhand's politics is shaped by differences between Garhwal and Kumaon, as well as the plains and Terai. The identities and local concerns of Garhwalis and Kumaonis form part of the state's political landscape, but they do not translate into fixed voting blocs. Employment, migration, land rights, infrastructure and access to public services can carry different weight across districts. The plains and Terai, meanwhile, have distinct demographic and economic dynamics. Congress will need to build a campaign that addresses these regional differences rather than assume that a single statewide message will resonate equally across all 70 constituencies.But the most dire step that Congress needs to take is to reconcile its senior leadership with the push for a more coordinated and visible state unit. The party can raise all the issues they want but unlike the BJP, they no longer have an established face to lead their campaigns. To put it lightly, their established faces have lost face during the previous elections.The BJP has already made Congress's internal differences part of its political argument. The Congress, in turn, is seeking to make governance and accountability the focus of the contest. Whether it can sustain that approach through a coordinated campaign, a stronger presence across constituencies and a clear leadership structure will be one of the defining questions of 2027.The BJP is seeking to make the election a referendum on continuity: its record in office, the leadership of Pushkar Singh Dhami, infrastructure development, welfare and the UCC.The Congress is trying to frame the election around accountability, employment, recruitment, migration, land and women’s safety.But the contest will ultimately be shaped by how voters across the state assess these competing claims. The BJP has the advantage of an established organisation and a second consecutive term behind it. The Congress has a list of grievances it hopes to turn into a campaign, but must still demonstrate that it can offer a coordinated alternative.The hills have eyes. They have watched governments come and go, and now they decide who they watch for the next 5 years.
Article Summary: BJP has a historic second but can it pull off a third? Congress wants a comeback. But can the Congress capitalise on anti-incumbency against the Dhami government to wrest back power and add another state to its tally? Uttarakhand is also a state where narrow margins have shaped constituency results.

Article Title: Sonia Gandhi was 'shocked' by Pranab Mukherjee's 'long-held desire' to be PM; his daughter asks why
Article Text:
Sonia on Pranab's PM ambition (PTI file photo)

Sonia on power-sharing with Manmohan Singh

What Sonia wrote about Pranab Mukherjee

Sonia rejects 'back-seat driver' charge

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Former Congress chief Sonia Gandhi has recounted how senior party colleague Pranab Mukherjee hinted at his "long-held desire" to become prime minister during a conversation in 2010, leaving her "shocked" with the suggestion that perhaps "it was time for a change at the top. "The account in her newly released memoir, however, has drawn a sharp response from Pranab Mukherjee's daughter Sharmistha, who questioned why her father's ambition could have come as a surprise.Responding to Sonia's memoir, "Belonging: A Journey of Love", Sharmishtha said there was nothing wrong with a politician aspiring to become prime minister, particularly someone with her father's experience in politics and governance."What's there to get 'shocked' about? Is it a crime to be ambitious, especially when that 'ambition' was supported by decades of experience in politics & governance, hard work & a brilliant mind?" she said.Recalling a conversation with her father, Sharmistha said she had once asked him whether he wanted to become prime minister. He had candidly replied that "any politician worth his salt has this ambition"."My father came from a very humble background. Whatever he achieved in his life was through sheer merit & hard-work.There was no-one to serve him positions, including PM-ship, on a platter due to dynastic entitlements. If a well-deserving person harbours ambition to become Prime Minister, what's wrong in that, unless Sonia ji was 'shocked' by the fact that anyone outside Gandhi-Nehru family could even dare to nurture such an ambition & furthermore dared to 'hint' it to her?" she said.Sharmistha also responded to Sonia's claim that Pranab Mukherjee never made her feel he held her response against him after she changed the subject during their conversation."In this same context, I read that she said she felt 'he never held it against me'. From what I read in his diaries & whatever conversation he had with me, I would like to reassure her that he DID NOT hold it against her or anyone else. He was a pragmatic person with deep understanding. He understood her reasons & insecurities that all human beings are prone to," she said.Also read: Sonia Gandhi memoir: BJP's Phoolka questions Army timeline, Indira's tears on 1984 riots In her memoir, Sonia writes that she was clear about Manmohan Singh being the prime minister and that, while she could offer him her opinions and suggestions as Congress president or disagree with him, it was her duty to defer to him."Further. I was determined not to be under any circumstance the cause of a misunderstanding that could give our opponents occasion to rejoice and weaken our government," she says in the book, which hit the stands on Tuesday.Former Congress chief describes an "unspoken division of responsibility" between the prime minister and herself, which she says worked smoothly: "the government under Dr. Manmohan Singh, and the party under me".She also recounts how the Congress leadership coordinated with the government through a core group that met weekly with the prime minister."A core group met weekly with the prime minister to ensure coordination between the two. Its other members were Pranab Mukherjee, who had been a minister in Indira Gandhi's cabinet in the 70s; the politically insightful Arjun Singh, a former chief minister of Madhya Pradesh; A K Anthony, a former chief minister of Kerala: and Ahmed Patel," she writes."We also met regularly as members of the Strategy Group, set up to discuss issues to be taken up in Parliament. Sometimes Pranab ji, as I always called him, would stay back for a chat," she says.Sonia recalls that Pranab Mukherjee had developed serious differences with then-finance minister P Chidambaram. During one such conversation in 2010, after expressing his frustration, Pranab made the suggestion that "surprised" her."He (Pranab) had developed serious differences with the finance minister P Chidambaram, and on one occasion, in 2010, I think after expressing his frustration, he shocked me with the suggestion that perhaps it was time for a change at the top, which I understood as a hint of his long-held desire to become prime minister," Rajya Sabha member Sonia Gandhi says."I gently changed the subject, and though he may have been disappointed, he never made me feel he held it against me," she adds.Sonia points out that the Congress later nominated Pranab Mukherjee as the UPA's presidential candidate in 2012. He went on to win the election and become the President of India."I often called on him, mostly just to converse with the erudite and knowledgeable politician that he always remained."Addressing allegations that she wielded the real power during the UPA years, when Manmohan Singh served as prime minister from 2004 to 2014, Sonia refers to what she describes as a "rash of stories" in the media. She says some of these accounts were fed by people close to the prime minister."A decade later, a book was published by one of his former aides, reaffirming the malicious and totally false allegations spread all along by my opponents: That I sent for files from the prime minister's office (PMO), interfered with administrative matters, and made key appointments," she says, rejecting the BJP's repeated charge.Sonia says the allegations that she interfered in the functioning of the government were particularly distressing, as she had always been careful to follow established rules."Though I had been the subject of worse accusations over the years, the fabrication that distressed me most was that I was looking into official files something improper for anyone outside the government. I had always been particular about adhering to rules, all the more so during this period," she says.She adds that the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) had issued a statement categorically denying that official files had ever been shown to her.Sonia also cites an interview in which Manmohan Singh's daughter Upinder Singh criticised a book by one of his former aides, describing it as a betrayal of trust and defending the relationship between her father and the Congress leader."Dr. Manmohan Singh's daughter Upinder Singh in an interview called the book 'nothing but a stab in the back. . . a huge betrayal of trust' and 'a mischievous, unethical exercise'. She affirmed that her father's relationship with me was one of 'mutual trust and respect'. However, the opposition and the media looked for every opportunity to spin the narrative that I was the government's 'back-seat driver'," Sonia says.She also gave details on why she turned down PM post after UPA victory in 2004.
Article Summary: Pranab Mukherjee's daughter Sharmistha questions why her father's ambition could have come as a surprise. Sharmishtha says there was nothing wrong with a politician aspiring to become prime minister. Former Congress chief describes an "unspoken division of responsibility" between the prime minister and herself, which she says worked smoothly.

Article Title: 'No real contact with him': Sonia Gandhi recalls face-to-face meetings with PM Modi in memoir

‘We come from different ideological worlds’

Sonia Gandhi on PM Modi's rise within the RSS

‘Coarse language’ and attacks on opposition in Parliament

‘Congress-free India’: Sonia on BJP's opposition to Congress

Sonia Gandhi recalls 2002 Gujarat riots

Sonia Gandhi on her understanding of Hinduism and faith

NEW DELHI: Former Congress president Sonia Gandhi, in her memoir, has said that she has had "practically no real contact" with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, despite his more than 12 years in office. She writes that PM Modi tends to look away and avoid eye contact when they come face-to-face.In her memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi said their interactions were largely limited to formal greetings at official gatherings and brief exchanges about her health.Describing their occasional encounters, Sonia said they usually meet at semi-official gatherings, such as the meetings of major political party leaders in the Speaker's chamber at the end of Parliament sessions."It's a very small room, and usually many people are present, but when he comes face-to-face with me, we greet each other with a formal namaste. This is different from the past, when leaders across party divides would treat one another with cordiality. He tends to look away, avoiding eye contact," she wrote.Sonia Gandhi recalled that PM Modi had occasionally enquired about her health after she returned from a hospital stay.He asked, "Theek hain aap?" to which she would reply, "Jee, ab main theek hoon, shukriya.""Apart from such brief exchanges, we have never really conversed, though we've exchanged formal birthday and New Year greetings over the years," she added.Sonia Gandhi said her limited interaction with PM Modi was also set against a wider ideological divide between the two leaders. She described their political rivalry as a contest between contrasting visions of India, rather than a personal feud."We come from different ideological worlds; his idea of this country is vastly different from mine," she wrote.Explaining the difference, Sonia said, "All I learnt about India was assimilated from the members of my family, their lives of service, and their faith in a nation that encompassed a host of races and cultures, languages and faiths, based on principles of liberty and equality for all."On the contrary, she said PM Modi's vision of India was shaped by the RSS and his upbringing."Narendra Modi’s idea of India was constructed by the ideologues of the RSS and the experience of his own growing up. It affirmed a fundamentalism in which his faith and culture superseded all others. In that India, hierarchy, order, and control are central."Sonia said she stood for an India based on inclusiveness, secularism and social justice."He was fighting for his vision of India, and I for mine: an India against hegemony, an India that stands for inclusiveness, secularism, and social justice. It wasn't personal," she wrote.Sonia acknowledged that PM Modi had worked his way up within the RSS from an underprivileged background. However, she questioned the way his humble origins had been portrayed by his public relations team."Modi's origins may not have been as humble as his PR team has made out in marketing his image, but he had certainly worked his way to power within the RSS from an underprivileged world," she wrote.She also said PM Modi's political journey had been very different from hers. However, she found herself able to understand some of his discomfort with the ruling elite.Recalling her own experiences in Delhi's political circles, Sonia Gandhi said she often felt out of place during discussions in privileged drawing rooms. The views expressed there, she said, were far removed from the realities of ordinary Indians.She added that the suffering and struggle for survival she had witnessed in her constituency and during her travels across the country were unimaginable to this privileged group.Sonia Gandhi also criticised PM Modi's language in Parliament, alleging that he sometimes uses the same coarse language he employs at public rallies."When speaking in Parliament, he at times uses the same coarse language he employs in addressing a public rally. Much of the time he derides the opposition in what can only be termed a tirade," she wrote.She also accused the BJP of repeatedly targeting India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, for establishing the country's democratic and secular foundations."Jawaharlal Nehru, our first prime minister, is a particular target of his party's hostility, for having set our country on a democratic and secular course," Sonia wrote.She further alleged that Sangh Parivar websites were filled with malicious abuse and falsehoods against Nehru.Sonia Gandhi described the BJP's stated goal of a "Congress-free India" as an attempt to eliminate not just the party but also its policies and ideology.She said she believed the hostility towards Congress stemmed from the prime minister's conditioning by the RSS."I tend to believe that this antipathy stems from the conditioning of the prime minister by the RSS. It has inculcated in its cadre a commitment to an exclusionary, hardened version of Hinduism that has been crafted into a political agenda," she wrote.Sonia Gandhi also revisited the 2002 Gujarat riots, which took place when PM Modi was the state's chief minister.Recalling the violence that followed the Godhra train tragedy, she said the Sabarmati Express was returning to Ahmedabad from Ayodhya with Hindu kar sevaks when four coaches caught fire. Fifty-nine pilgrims were killed. She noted that the cause of the fire remained disputed, while the communal violence that followed spread to several parts of Gujarat and claimed predominantly Muslim victims."When I was leader of the opposition in Parliament, I met the victims of many tragedies, and each time I was haunted by the misery I had witnessed," she wrote.She recalled watching television reports of the violence and trying to reach Congress colleagues in Gujarat who were seeking help."We watched the live reports in horror, and tried to get help to our colleagues in Gujarat who were calling us in desperation, but the administration failed to respond," she wrote.Sonia Gandhi said the riots were reported to have been fuelled by a fanatical fringe of the BJP and RSS, including the Bajrang Dal. PM Modi was the chief minister of Gujarat at the time.Sonia also contrasted the RSS's political interpretation of Hinduism with the inclusive understanding of faith she said she had learnt from her mother-in-law.She described this understanding as one that embraced different beliefs and paths, without being tied to a single deity, dogma, prophet or scripture."What I learnt from my mother-in-law is the faith that's been practised for centuries in India by vast numbers of our people -- from stalwarts of the freedom struggle to the poorest in our villages. It embraces diverse beliefs and different paths, adheres to no single deity, dogma, prophet, or scripture, and has included traditions of dissent," she wrote.She added that she had been educated in the principles of ahimsa and dharma as interpreted by Mahatma Gandhi. She also acknowledged the oppression and inequality associated with India's caste system, while pointing out that reformers had used ideas within Hinduism to challenge caste discrimination.
Article Summary: Former Congress president Sonia Gandhi has said she has had "practically no real contact" with Prime Minister Narendra Modi. She writes that PM Modi tends to look away and avoid eye contact when they come face-to-face. She also criticised PM Modi's language in Parliament, alleging that he sometimes uses the same coarse language he employs at public rallies.

Article Title: 'I'd quake in my seat': Sonia Gandhi recalls Indira Gandhi's temper, early days as bride in memoir
Article Text:
Sonia recalls Indira Gandhi's temper

Indira's love for old photographs, sarees and shawls

NEW DELHI: A staffer made to stand in a corner, a senior Congress leader ordered to face the wall and another person ignored for days. Indira Gandhi had different ways of dealing with those who triggered her “occasional explosions of temper”, Sonia Gandhi writes in her recently released memoir, recalling her early days as a bride in the Nehru-Gandhi family.In her much-anticipated memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, the senior Congress leader offers a glimpse into the temperament of the former prime minister and her mother-in-law, describing how her sudden outbursts could leave even those around her visibly shaken.The 544-page book, published by HarperCollins India, traces the arc of Sonia's life, from her childhood in post-war Italy and marriage into the Nehru-Gandhi family to the assassination of her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, and her eventual entry into politics.Also Read| What made Sonia Gandhi turn down PM post after UPA’s 2004 victory? Memoir revisits moment “What I found most alarming was my mother-in-law's occasional explosions of temper. They could freeze the staff into numbness,” she writes.Recalling one such incident, Sonia says a staff member who had repeatedly forgotten to remind Indira of an important appointment was made to stand in a corner of the room as others hurriedly moved around him, visibly embarrassed.In another instance, she came across a “kurta-dhoti-clad individual standing immobile in the corner, staring at the wall”.“I was not yet familiar with who was who in the political pantheon, but the fact that he was within our private space signalled that he must have been a Congress Party senior,” she writes.Sonia recalls spending nearly half an hour with Amie Aunty, a senior member of Indira's staff, before returning to find the man still standing in the same position.Also Read| 'Should've called it Whitewashing, not Belonging': BJP mocks Sonia Gandhi's memoir “When I walked back, the man in white was still stuck to the wall as ordered by my mother-in-law, I learnt later,” she writes.Indira also had another way of expressing her displeasure: Refusing to acknowledge someone altogether. Sonia says there were occasions when the former prime minister would ignore an “offending individual”, leaving them in suspense for days.Her temper could also flare up at the dining table, particularly after a “particularly unpleasant exchange with the opposition” in Parliament. On one such occasion, Indira pushed her thali to the other side of the long dining table in a “fit of anger”.Sonia says these outbursts unsettled her, reminding her of her own father's temper. While she would feel perturbed and shaken, Rajiv and his younger brother Sanjay would sit quietly, waiting for the moment to pass.Rajiv would often reassure her: “Don't let yourself get so scared. She'll be all right in no time.”But such assurances did little to ease her anxiety in the early days of the marriage.“But until I got to know her well, I'd quake in my seat,” Sonia writes.She adds that Indira would usually regret her outbursts and find ways to communicate her remorse to those she had upset. However, she was far less forgiving when she felt a colleague had betrayed her trust.“She'd distance herself and not ever deal with that person again,” Sonia recalls.Beyond her moments of anger, Sonia also describes the domestic routines through which Indira found comfort and relaxation.One of her favourite activities was asking Amie Crishna to bring out boxes of old photographs, which she would then carefully sort by date. At other times, she would take out her sarees and, with the family's help, arrange them according to their provenance, attaching tags to each bundle for easy access.She would also set aside sarees that she had worn only occasionally but which were still in good condition, asking the family to make separate bundles for different relatives.Sonia also writes about Indira's fondness for sarees and old Kashmiri shawls, including several treasured sarees that had belonged to her mother from the pre-khadi period.The frequency of Indira's “tense moments” gradually declined after she became a grandmother.As her grandchildren grew older, they would often be sent to gauge her mood before approaching her. Their presence, Sonia writes, had a calming effect on the former prime minister.“A smile or an innocent question from her grandchildren at once melted her; they helped her to relax and provided much contentedness,” she writes.
Article Summary: Sonia recalls Indira Gandhi's temper in her memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love. She recalls how her sudden outbursts could leave even those around her visibly shaken. Sonia also writes about Indira's fondness for sarees and treasured shawls, including several treasured sarees that belonged to her mother.

Article Title: Arpita Singh, celebrated artist who painted real women, dies at 89
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Some critics dubbed her the female M F Husain while others saw echoes of Marc Chagall in her gravity-defying figures. But neither comparison does justice to the distinctive visual language of Arpita Singh, a pioneering post-Independence artist who died in Delhi on Monday at the age of 89.She looked like the friendly aunty next door, but her canvases were another matter. In one famous painting titled Devi Pistol Wali, a many-armed Durga holds a saree pallu, flowers and fruit, while another hand aims a revolver. My Lily Pond’s serenity is shattered by toy soldiers. Across her canvases, the macabre and the mundane, fantasy and reality, share space.When this reporter met her at a Vadehra Art Gallery show some years ago, she had been poring over old maps and architectural drawings, studying the stars and solving crosswords. “I gather things on canvas. When I finish gathering, I start painting,” she said. She could not predict what would end up in a work. “They take a shape of their own.” Her paintings often feel like riddles, asking the viewer to follow her cryptic clues and come to their own answers. She disliked explaining her own art. “There should be a difference between what the viewer sees and what the artist paints.”Asked why her women were often middle-aged, unvarnished and un-eroticised, Singh’s answer was plain: “I don’t decide in advance whether the woman is going to be thin or fat, pretty or ugly.Anyway, glamorous women with hourglass shapes are for film and television. I paint real women.”Roobina Karode, chief curator of the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art, put together a retrospective of her work in 2019 to showcase the breadth of her oeuvre. “Her sharp wit, humour and provocations drew inspiration from entangled and chaotic everyday life, amplifying the pressures of contrary forces from a woman’s vantage point,” said Karode.Women were central to her work, but Singh did not treat them as symbols to be decoded. They could be vulnerable and formidable, funny, exhausted and unsettling. The 1990 Devi Pistol Wali caused quite a stir when it was published in a Durga Puja issue of Ananda Bazar Patrika.She was alert to the violence around her, and unwilling to leave it outside the studio. “We live in violent times, and as an artist, I can’t escape that,” she had said. “It stares at me from the front pages of every newspaper and the cover of every news magazine.” Her paintings could connect present-day violence to older histories, while making room for the ordinary objects that marked a life. Sofa sets, potted plants, bouquets and kitchen utensils became, in her words, “my signposts”.Born in Baranagar, Bengal, Singh moved from Calcutta to New Delhi at ten, after her father died. Her school principal persuaded her mother that her daughter’s talent for making charts could benefit from formal art training. Singh earned a diploma in fine arts from Delhi Polytechnic in 1959. In the mid-1960s, she spent four years as a designer at the Weavers’ Service Centre. The interest in textiles, pattern and embroidery shaped her art.In 1985, when Nalini Malani’s plan for a women-only exhibition lost its sponsors, Singh joined Malani, Madhvi Parekh and Nilima Sheikh in pooling money to stage it.In 2010, her 16-panel mural Wish Dream fetched Rs 9.56 crore at Saffronart, then a record price at auction for an Indian woman artist. She received the Padma Bhushan in 2011 and a Lalit Kala Akademi fellowship in 2014. In 2025, London’s Serpentine presented Remembering, her first institutional solo exhibition outside India. She is survived by her husband, the artist Paramjit Singh. Their artist-daughter, Anjum Singh, died of cancer in 2020.
Article Summary: Arpita Singh, a pioneering post-Independence artist, died in Delhi on Monday at the age of 89. In one famous painting titled Devi Pistol Wali, a many-armed Durga holds a saree pallu, flowers and fruit, while another hand aims a revolver. Her paintings often feel like riddles, asking the viewer to follow her cryptic clues.

Article Title: Delhi records 'very poor' air quality on Diwali, 19 monitoring stations report severe AQI
Article Text:

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think firecracker emissions should be banned during festivals? Yes, completely Yes, with restrictions No, it's part of tradition 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Delhi's Air Quality Index stood at 371, in the 'very poor' category, on Sunday evening as people stepped out to celebrate DiwaliThe national capital witnessed a further deterioration in air quality as firecracker emissions added to the existing pollution burden. Several residents took to social media platform X to report a smoky smell and hazy conditions in different parts of the city, with some also complaining of reduced visibility.Data from 59 air quality monitoring stations across Delhi painted a grim picture. At 7 pm, 19 stations had recorded 'severe' air quality, while 33 were in the 'very poor' category. The remaining seven stations reported 'poor' air quality.Jahangirpuri emerged as the most polluted location, recording an AQI of 460, placing it firmly in the 'severe' category.Delhi's average AQI for the day was 376, up from 369 on Saturday, indicating a worsening pollution situation ahead of the festival's peak celebrations.The deterioration is expected to continue, with the Air Quality Early Warning System (EWS) forecasting that the city's air quality could slip into the 'severe' category from November 9 and remain there for the next few days.The spike comes as multiple sources of pollution are converging.Firecracker emissions, vehicular exhaust and stubble burning in neighbouring states are expected to compound the problem, while unfavourable weather conditions could prevent pollutants from dispersing.The EWS has flagged poor ventilation conditions as a major concern. A ventilation index below 6,000 square metres per second, along with average wind speeds of less than 10 kilometres per hour, is considered unfavourable for the dispersal of pollutants.PM2.5 remained the dominant pollutant in Delhi on Sunday, with firecracker emissions adding to the concentration of fine particulate matter in the air.According to the Decision Support System (DSS) for Delhi, the transport sector was expected to account for the largest share of the city's pollution load on Sunday, contributing 19 per cent.The contribution from stubble burning was estimated at 3.5 per cent on Sunday and is projected to decline slightly to around 2.99 per cent on Monday.
Article Summary: Jahangirpuri emerged as the most polluted location, recording an AQI of 460, placing it firmly in the'severe' category. The average AQI for the day was 376, up from 369 on Saturday, indicating a worsening pollution situation ahead of the festival's peak celebrations.

Article Title: Presidential election today? Trump confuses India with Brazil, claims 125 million voted
Article Text:
Trump says "125 million Indians voted in presidential election today."

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

US President Donald Trump on Monday confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian “presidential election”, while also questioning the integrity of the American voting system.In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “125 Million People voted today in the first round of India’s Presidential Election. The results came out shortly after the vote closed, on the same day!”He then compared the alleged election results with the US electoral process, writing, “In Detroit, Philadelphia, California, and numerous other US Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate. Voting in America is corrupt!!!”However, India did not hold a presidential election on Sunday. The President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral college and not through a direct nationwide popular vote.Trump's remarks came after Brazil held the first round of its presidential election on Sunday, with incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro advancing to the October 25 runoff.With 99.99% of the votes counted, Bolsonaro secured 47.03% of the valid votes, while Lula received 45.16%, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.The figure of around 125 million mentioned by Trump is close to Brazil's total valid votes, which stood at about 125.27 million, suggesting he may have confused the Brazilian election with India.Neither Bolsonaro nor Lula crossed the 50% threshold required to win in the first round, triggering the October 25 runoff, BBC reported.Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, outperformed expectations in the first round and finished ahead of Lula. His strong showing has raised the prospect of a shift to the right in Latin America's largest economy.Brazil has used electronic voting for decades, and electoral authorities said the first-round voting process proceeded smoothly.The Organization of American States' electoral observation mission said “the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions.”The rapid announcement of results has also been cited as a strength of Brazil's electronic voting system.“When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there’s been a problem,” Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, told the Associated Press.Trump's post drew reactions on social media, with users pointing out that India does not elect its president through a direct popular vote.One user posted, “Trump living in a different world? Is a presidential election taking place in India? President Donald Trump made the incorrect claim that 125 million people voted in India's "presidential election" today.”Another said, “What is my blud Donald Trump smoking? Why is he mentioning India instead of Brazil when talking about the election?”
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian "presidential election" He also questioned the integrity of the American voting system. India did not hold a presidential election on Sunday. The President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral college.

Article Title: ‘It's a wee bit of frustration’: Kyle Jamieson flags New Zealand’s injury-hit bowling attack against India
Article Text:
New Zealand's Kyle Jamieson celebrates the wicket of India's Shreyas Iyer during the 2nd ODI. (AP/PTI Photo)

Injuries disrupt New Zealand's bowling plans

Jamieson enjoys conditions offering help to bowlers

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: New Zealand pacer Kyle Jamieson has admitted that the hosts' inability to field a settled bowling attack has been a source of frustration during the ongoing white-ball series against India, with injuries disrupting their plans and affecting the team's ability to build consistency.New Zealand lost the five-match T20I series 2-3 and are trailing 0-2 in the five-match ODI series, with the third match abandoned due to inclement weather. The hosts have been without senior pacers Matt Henry and Lockie Ferguson , while Blair Tickner also suffered an injury during the second ODI.Jamieson believes the repeated changes to the bowling combination have prevented the attack from developing the cohesion needed to challenge India consistently.“It's a wee bit of frustration, right? You're trying to always put a similar attack out and you sort of can build that camaraderie and build that cohesion. We haven't had the reps (repetitions) that we'd like. But hopefully over the next couple of weeks we'll sort of all come out here together and get a good run of cricket together,” Jamieson was quoted as saying by the host broadcasters before the toss in the third ODI.The absence of Henry and Ferguson has deprived New Zealand of two experienced fast-bowling options, while Tickner's injury has further complicated their plans.The lack of continuity has been particularly challenging against an Indian batting line-up that has capitalised on the hosts' bowling changes.Jamieson, however, has been among the more effective performers for New Zealand. He troubled India's batters with seam movement and bounce in Wellington, claiming three wickets in the rain-affected contest.“Just trying to manage a little bit of the weather stuff. Trying to get it right on what conditions are going to look like and just trying to put them (opposition) under a little bit of pressure,” he said.The tall pacer also welcomed the conditions in the series, which have offered assistance to the bowlers, contrasting them with batting-friendly surfaces where restricting the opposition to a run rate below 10 is considered a good effort.“No, I love it. I'm so used to like these wickets that are, you know, if you go under tens, you're having a good day. So it's nice to have a little bit in your favour. You can kind of just try and land on a spot and hope you get a little bit of assistance. So, it's nice to have a little bit more in our favour. And long may that continue,” he said.With a demanding run of Test cricket ahead, Jamieson also spoke about the adjustment required when switching from white-ball cricket to the longer format.“It takes a while but just trying to trust the work that you've done, trust the process around it and then just ultimately just sort of surrender into the game, into what may or may not happen,” he said.The pacer added that managing his physical condition had been a major focus during his time away from the game.“I kind of always felt like my game was in an okay space. It was just trying to get the physical and the body side of it sort of, a bit more under my control. I felt like if I could kind of put some of those steps in place, get a run of cricket under my belt, it was always going to be all right,” Jamieson said.“So thankfully I sort of feel like I'm coming out the other side of it now and obviously a big run of Test cricket coming up. So touch wood we survive that,” he added.
Article Summary: New Zealand's inability to field a settled bowling attack has been a source of frustration during the ongoing white-ball series against India. The hosts have been without senior pacers Matt Henry and Lockie Ferguson, while Blair Tickner also suffered an injury during the second ODI. Jamieson has been among the more effective performers for New Zealand.

Article Title: Patrick Mahomes' latest injury update brings relief to Chiefs fans after scary Jets moment
Article Text:
Patrick Mahomes (Image via Getty Images)

Andy Reid provides encouraging Patrick Mahomes injury update

"It was more positive news than negative news on Patrick,"

Patrick Mahomes' MRI reportedly reveals no major damage
